report:
## Conclusion

The best available evidence **does not support the claim that having an induced abortion increases breast-cancer risk**.

The concern arose from a biological hypothesis: early pregnancy stimulates breast-cell growth, while later pregnancy promotes differentiation into milk-producing cells; abortion was proposed to interrupt that protective process. Some early case-control studies also reported an association. A frequently cited 1996 meta-analysis combined 23 studies and concluded that induced abortion was an independent risk factor: https://jech.bmj.com/content/50/5/481

However, those studies generally asked women to recall past abortions after diagnosis. This design is vulnerable to reporting bias: women with breast cancer may disclose a past abortion more completely than women without cancer. Stronger prospective and registry-based research has not confirmed the association. A 2004 collaborative reanalysis of individual data from **53 studies in 16 countries**, including 83,000 women with breast cancer, found that neither induced nor spontaneous abortion increased risk; it concluded that retrospective studies had produced misleading results: https://www.thelancet.com/journals/lancet/article/PIIS0140-6736(04)15835-2/fulltext

In 2003, the U.S. National Cancer Institute convened more than 100 experts to review the evidence. It concluded that induced abortion is **not associated** with increased breast-cancer risk: https://www.cancer.gov/types/breast/abortion-miscarriage-risk

The American Cancer Society similarly reports that expert reviews by NCI and ACOG found no causal relationship: https://www.cancer.org/cancer/risk-prevention/medical-treatments/abortion-and-breast-cancer-risk.html

Thus, although the claim has a proposed mechanism and some supportive older studies, the higher-quality and more comprehensive evidence refutes it.
